questions.topicName: Development of the Gastrointestinal System
questions.stem: This four-step sequence shows the lumen of a developing gut segment being obliterated and then reopened. Complete failure of the reopening step in a segment results in which condition?

explanation.summary: Early in development the endodermal epithelium proliferates and occludes the lumen; recanalization then restores patency. If recanalization fails entirely, the segment remains a solid cord, producing atresia; if it is incomplete, stenosis results.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early in development the endodermal epithelium proliferates and occludes the lumen; recanalization then restores patency. If recanalization fails entirely, the segment remains a solid cord, producing atresia; if it is incomplete, stenosis results.

questions.topicName: Development of the Gastrointestinal System
questions.stem: The gut segment on the left retains a narrowed but still-patent lumen. This appearance results from which developmental error?

explanation.summary: Partial (incomplete) removal of the cells that had occluded the lumen leaves a narrowed but patent channel, i.e., stenosis. Complete failure of recanalization would instead produce atresia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Partial (incomplete) removal of the cells that had occluded the lumen leaves a narrowed but patent channel, i.e., stenosis. Complete failure of recanalization would instead produce atresia.

questions.topicName: Development of the Gastrointestinal System
questions.stem: This figure shows the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds fusing around the duodenum. If the ventral bud abnormally migrates so that pancreatic tissue completely encircles the duodenum, which condition results?

explanation.summary: Abnormal migration/rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud can cause pancreatic tissue to form a ring around the second part of the duodenum (annular pancreas), potentially causing duodenal obstruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Abnormal migration/rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud can cause pancreatic tissue to form a ring around the second part of the duodenum (annular pancreas), potentially causing duodenal obstruction.

questions.topicName: Development of the Gastrointestinal System
questions.stem: In this cross-section of the trilaminar embryo, the cavity that forms when the lateral plate mesoderm splits will become which adult structure?

explanation.summary: The intraembryonic coelom seen between the somatic and splanchnic mesoderm layers becomes the body cavities; in the abdomen it forms the peritoneal cavity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The intraembryonic coelom seen between the somatic and splanchnic mesoderm layers becomes the body cavities; in the abdomen it forms the peritoneal cavity.

questions.topicName: Development of the Gastrointestinal System
questions.stem: In this detailed embryo, the transverse mesodermal partition just cranial to the liver bud is highlighted. This structure is the primordium of which adult structure?

explanation.summary: The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm (and contributes to the ventral mesentery of the liver). Defective formation underlies congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm (and contributes to the ventral mesentery of the liver). Defective formation underlies congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

questions.topicName: Development of the Gastrointestinal System
questions.stem: These cross-sections illustrate the 90-degree clockwise rotation of the stomach. As a result of this rotation, which nerve comes to lie on the posterior surface of the stomach?

explanation.summary: Gastric rotation carries the right (originally right-sided) vagus posteriorly to form the posterior vagal trunk, while the left vagus becomes the anterior vagal trunk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastric rotation carries the right (originally right-sided) vagus posteriorly to form the posterior vagal trunk, while the left vagus becomes the anterior vagal trunk.

questions.topicName: Development of the Gastrointestinal System
questions.stem: The proximal duodenum shown here develops from two embryonic regions, giving it a dual blood supply. Besides branches of the celiac trunk, which artery supplies it?

explanation.summary: The duodenum straddles the foregut-midgut junction. The foregut portion is supplied by the celiac trunk and the midgut portion by the superior mesenteric artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: The duodenum straddles the foregut-midgut junction. The foregut portion is supplied by the celiac trunk and the midgut portion by the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.topicName: Development of the Gastrointestinal System
questions.stem: This sequence traces herniation and return of the midgut loop around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery. What is the total degree and direction of rotation completed by the end of this process?

explanation.summary: The midgut loop rotates a total of 270 degrees counterclockwise (when viewed from the front) around the SMA axis before and during its return to the abdomen. Failure of this rotation causes malrotation and predisposes to volvulus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The midgut loop rotates a total of 270 degrees counterclockwise (when viewed from the front) around the SMA axis before and during its return to the abdomen. Failure of this rotation causes malrotation and predisposes to volvulus.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: This schematic illustrates the embryologic origin of a pancreatic anomaly that can encircle and obstruct the second part of the duodenum. Which developmental error produces it?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abnormal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of the dorsal pancreatic bud to form

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of neural crest cell migration

explanation.summary: The pancreas forms from ventral and dorsal buds. If the ventral bud rotates abnormally, it can partially or completely encircle the duodenum (annular pancreas), sometimes causing duodenal obstruction with bilious vomiting and a double-bubble appearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pancreas forms from ventral and dorsal buds. If the ventral bud rotates abnormally, it can partially or completely encircle the duodenum (annular pancreas), sometimes causing duodenal obstruction with bilious vomiting and a double-bubble appearance.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: The right-hand panel of this diagram shows small bowel twisted around its vascular pedicle. Which underlying anatomic abnormality predisposes an infant to this complication?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A narrow mesenteric base from failed midgut rotation

explanation.summary: When the midgut fails to complete its normal 270-degree counterclockwise rotation, the mesentery anchors over a very short base rather than a broad one. This narrow pedicle allows the bowel to twist on itself (volvulus), compromising the superior mesenteric vessels and risking necrosis of the entire small intestine.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the midgut fails to complete its normal 270-degree counterclockwise rotation, the mesentery anchors over a very short base rather than a broad one. This narrow pedicle allows the bowel to twist on itself (volvulus), compromising the superior mesenteric vessels and risking necrosis of the entire small intestine.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: These illustrations depict variants in which the rectum connects abnormally to the urinary or genital tract. Faulty development of which septum accounts for this entire group of anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The transverse septum of the septum transversum

explanation.summary: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into anorectal and urogenital portions. Abnormal development leaves fistulous connections between the rectum and the urethra, bladder, or vestibule (and, at the extreme, a persistent cloaca), as illustrated across these variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into anorectal and urogenital portions. Abnormal development leaves fistulous connections between the rectum and the urethra, bladder, or vestibule (and, at the extreme, a persistent cloaca), as illustrated across these variants.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: These ultrasound images compare a normal pylorus (left) with an abnormal one (right, circled). Which sonographic feature confirms the diagnosis on the right?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A target/donut sign of telescoped bowel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bird-beak narrowing of the distal esophagus

choices.label: E
choices.text: A dilated aganglionic megacolon with transition zone

explanation.summary: Ultrasound is the confirmatory test for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, revealing an enlarged pylorus with increased muscle wall thickness (roughly >3 mm) and elongated channel length compared with the thin, short normal pylorus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ultrasound is the confirmatory test for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, revealing an enlarged pylorus with increased muscle wall thickness (roughly >3 mm) and elongated channel length compared with the thin, short normal pylorus.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: This upper GI contrast study of an infant shows a 'corkscrew' proximal small bowel that fails to cross to the left of the vertebral column. This finding confirms which diagnosis?

explanation.summary: In malrotation the duodenum lacks a normal C-loop and does not cross the midline; when volvulus occurs the proximal jejunum shows a classic corkscrew pattern. An upper GI study is the confirmatory test in a stable infant with bilious vomiting.
explanation.whyCorrect: In malrotation the duodenum lacks a normal C-loop and does not cross the midline; when volvulus occurs the proximal jejunum shows a classic corkscrew pattern. An upper GI study is the confirmatory test in a stable infant with bilious vomiting.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: This contrast enema shows a narrowed distal segment with an abrupt transition to markedly dilated proximal colon. What is the underlying cause of this appearance?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mesenteric vascular accident with segmental resorption

choices.label: D
choices.text: Twisting of bowel around a narrow mesentery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Absence of ganglion cells from failed neural crest migration

explanation.summary: In Hirschsprung disease, neural crest cells fail to migrate into the distal gut, leaving an aganglionic, tonically contracted segment (usually rectosigmoid). The narrowed aganglionic bowel cannot relax, so the normally innervated proximal colon dilates, creating the transition zone seen on contrast enema.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Hirschsprung disease, neural crest cells fail to migrate into the distal gut, leaving an aganglionic, tonically contracted segment (usually rectosigmoid). The narrowed aganglionic bowel cannot relax, so the normally innervated proximal colon dilates, creating the transition zone seen on contrast enema.

questions.topicName: Oral Dysbiosis: Microflora and Clinical Pathologies
questions.stem: This labeled cross-section shows an untreated tooth lesion that has progressed to the red collection at the root apex. Which organism is the primary initiator of the process that leads to this outcome?

explanation.summary: Dental caries are initiated by Streptococcus mutans, which ferments dietary sucrose into lactic acid and produces sticky glucans that demineralize enamel. Untreated caries progress through dentin into the pulp, causing pulp necrosis and eventually a periapical (dental) abscess, as depicted.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dental caries are initiated by Streptococcus mutans, which ferments dietary sucrose into lactic acid and produces sticky glucans that demineralize enamel. Untreated caries progress through dentin into the pulp, causing pulp necrosis and eventually a periapical (dental) abscess, as depicted.

questions.topicName: Oral Dysbiosis: Microflora and Clinical Pathologies
questions.stem: White plaques that scrape off to reveal an erythematous base are shown in this infant's mouth. Which organism is responsible?

explanation.summary: Oral thrush (pseudomembranous candidiasis) is caused by Candida albicans and produces scrapable white plaques on the oral mucosa. It typically arises with immunosuppression, antibiotic use, or inhaled corticosteroid therapy. Scrapability distinguishes it from hairy leukoplakia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oral thrush (pseudomembranous candidiasis) is caused by Candida albicans and produces scrapable white plaques on the oral mucosa. It typically arises with immunosuppression, antibiotic use, or inhaled corticosteroid therapy. Scrapability distinguishes it from hairy leukoplakia.

questions.topicName: Oral Dysbiosis: Microflora and Clinical Pathologies
questions.stem: This non-scrapable, corrugated white lesion on the lateral tongue is most strongly associated with reactivation of which virus?

explanation.summary: Hairy leukoplakia produces non-scrapable, corrugated white patches on the lateral tongue and results from Epstein-Barr virus reactivation, characteristically in immunocompromised (e.g., HIV) patients. Unlike thrush, it cannot be wiped off.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hairy leukoplakia produces non-scrapable, corrugated white patches on the lateral tongue and results from Epstein-Barr virus reactivation, characteristically in immunocompromised (e.g., HIV) patients. Unlike thrush, it cannot be wiped off.

questions.topicName: Oral Dysbiosis: Microflora and Clinical Pathologies
questions.stem: This young child presents with the painful perioral and intraoral vesicular and ulcerative lesions shown. Which virus is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is caused by HSV-1 and typically presents in children 6 months to 5 years with painful oral vesicles that ulcerate and resolve within 1-2 weeks. A Tzanck smear may show multinucleated giant cells, though PCR is now preferred.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is caused by HSV-1 and typically presents in children 6 months to 5 years with painful oral vesicles that ulcerate and resolve within 1-2 weeks. A Tzanck smear may show multinucleated giant cells, though PCR is now preferred.

questions.topicName: Sjogren Syndrome
questions.stem: These high- and low-power views of a salivary gland from a patient with Sjogren syndrome show dense focal inflammatory aggregates (arrows) replacing acini. Which cell type predominates within these infiltrates?

explanation.summary: The histologic hallmark of Sjogren syndrome is focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, in which periductal/periacinar aggregates are composed predominantly of CD4+ T cells (with B cells), quantified as a focus score on labial gland biopsy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The histologic hallmark of Sjogren syndrome is focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, in which periductal/periacinar aggregates are composed predominantly of CD4+ T cells (with B cells), quantified as a focus score on labial gland biopsy.

questions.topicName: Sjogren Syndrome
questions.stem: This clinical photograph shows the dry, fissured tongue of a patient with Sjogren syndrome. Which underlying change most directly accounts for this oral finding?

explanation.summary: Lymphocytic destruction of salivary gland acini reduces saliva output (xerostomia), leaving the mucosa dry and fissured and predisposing to candidal overgrowth and angular cheilitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymphocytic destruction of salivary gland acini reduces saliva output (xerostomia), leaving the mucosa dry and fissured and predisposing to candidal overgrowth and angular cheilitis.
